- **Total de atores indicados:** Aproximadamente 50+ nomes principais

- **Principais nacionalidades:** Americano, Irlandês, Britânico, Australiano, Alemão, Espanhol, Japonês

### 82º Golden Globe Awards (2025)
- **Total de atores indicados:** Aproximadamente 30+ nomes principais
- **Destaque:** Karla Sofía Gascón (primeira transgênero a ser indicada para um prêmio de atuação em filme), Sofía Vergara (colombiana), e Jodie Foster (novamente indicada)

Este relatório apresenta um panorama completo dos atores indicados tanto ao 81º quanto ao 82º Golden Globe Awards, com informações detalhadas sobre ano de nascimento e nacionalidade. Os dois eventos destacaram uma diversidade significativa de talentos internacionais, refletindo a evolução da indústria cinematográfica e televisiva em direção a maior inclusão. A presença de atores de diferentes origens culturais — desde os Estados Unidos até o Japão, México, Colômbia, Austrália e Europa — demonstra a natureza globalizada das premiações de Hollywood.

The **81st Golden Globe Awards** was an awards ceremony for [film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_film "2023 in film") and [American television productions of 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_American_television "2023 in American television"). It was broadcast live on January 7, 2024, from [the Beverly Hilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beverly_Hilton "The Beverly Hilton") in [Beverly Hills, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills,_California "Beverly Hills, California"), beginning at 5:00 p.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") / 8:00 p.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone"), on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") and streamed on [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") in the United States. It was produced by [Dick Clark Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Clark_Productions "Dick Clark Productions"), [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner"), and [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss"); the latter also served as director.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Otterson-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Donnelly-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Schneider-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Winners-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Winners_List-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-8) This was the first ceremony after Dick Clark Productions and [Eldridge Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldridge_Industries "Eldridge Industries") took full control of the Golden Globes from the [Hollywood Foreign Press Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Foreign_Press_Association "Hollywood Foreign Press Association").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Otterson-1) The ceremony was also the first to air live on CBS in the United States since [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/39th_Golden_Globe_Awards "39th Golden Globe Awards").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Otterson-1) Comedian [Jo Koy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Koy "Jo Koy") hosted the ceremony.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Host-2)

The nominees were announced on December 11, 2023. *[Barbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbie_(film) "Barbie (film)")* and *[Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_(TV_series) "Succession (TV series)")* both tied for the most nominations with nine each, followed by *[Oppenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppenheimer_(film) "Oppenheimer (film)")*'s eight.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Nominees-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Barbenheimer-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-11)

The ceremony also featured the debut of two new categories: "[Cinematic and Box Office Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Cinematic_and_Box_Office_Achievement "Golden Globe Award for Cinematic and Box Office Achievement")" and "[Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Performance_in_Stand-Up_Comedy_on_Television "Golden Globe Award for Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television")"[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-New_Categories-12)

Additionally, the cultural phenomenon of "[Barbenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbenheimer "Barbenheimer")" received seventeen nominations, winning seven.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Winners-6)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Barbenheimer-10)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-15)

## Ceremony information

This was the first Golden Globe Awards ceremony after the [Hollywood Foreign Press Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Foreign_Press_Association "Hollywood Foreign Press Association") (HFPA) disbanded in 2023. On June 12, 2023, the HFPA announced that all of its rights and properties related to the Golden Globes were acquired by [Dick Clark Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Clark_Productions "Dick Clark Productions") and [Eldridge Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldridge_Industries "Eldridge Industries").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-16)

On February 21, 2023, the date of the ceremony was announced. It came back on a Sunday night slot after being moved to Tuesday for the previous year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Donnelly-4) On September 18, 2023, [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") and [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") were announced as its executive producers and showrunners.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Schneider-5) On November 17, 2023, it was announced that [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") had acquired the broadcast rights to the ceremony, replacing the Golden Globes' long-time U.S. broadcast partner [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Otterson-1)

The nominations were announced on December 11, 2023, during an event co-hosted by [Cedric the Entertainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedric_the_Entertainer "Cedric the Entertainer") and [Wilmer Valderrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmer_Valderrama "Wilmer Valderrama"). Most of the categories were revealed during a live-streaming presentation, while ten of the categories were revealed during another segment on *[CBS Mornings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Mornings "CBS Mornings")*.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Nominees-9)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-18)

On December 21, comedian and actor [Jo Koy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Koy "Jo Koy") was announced as the host.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Host-2)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-22) Before this announcement, it was reported that a source with knowledge of the conversations told [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") that at least five A-list comedic actors, including [Chris Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Rock "Chris Rock") and [Ali Wong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Wong "Ali Wong"), declined offers to host; the hosts of the podcast *[SmartLess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SmartLess "SmartLess")* (actors [Will Arnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Arnett "Will Arnett"), [Jason Bateman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Bateman "Jason Bateman"), and [Sean Hayes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Hayes "Sean Hayes")) also reportedly declined the offer.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-23) That same month, *[TheWrap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TheWrap "TheWrap")* reported that 64 voters threatened to withhold their final-round votes in protest, after being told that they would not be given tickets to the ceremony.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-24)

With the awards no longer being overseen by the HFPA, a new, racially and ethnically diverse group of voters consisting of 300 journalists representing 76 countries selected the 2023 nominees and winners.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Winners_List-7)

For her portrayal of [Mollie Burkhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollie_Kyle "Mollie Kyle") in *[Killers of the Flower Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killers_of_the_Flower_Moon "Killers of the Flower Moon")*, [Lily Gladstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lily_Gladstone "Lily Gladstone") became the first [Indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") actor to win a Golden Globe Award, winning for [Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actress_in_a_Motion_Picture_–_Drama "Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Drama").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-25)

### Expansion

On September 26, 2023, it was announced that two new categories would be added for the upcoming ceremony: "[Cinematic and Box Office Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Cinematic_and_Box_Office_Achievement "Golden Globe Award for Cinematic and Box Office Achievement")" (a category for films that grossed at least $100 million domestically and $150 million worldwide) and "[Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Performance_in_Stand-Up_Comedy_on_Television "Golden Globe Award for Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television")" (also known as "Best Stand-Up Comedian on Television").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-New_Categories-12)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-29) Some critics felt that the new categories were an attempt to improve the ceremony's viewership and relevance, with comparisons drawn to the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards")' [attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/91st_Academy_Awards#Proposed_"Popular_Film"_category "91st Academy Awards") to introduce a [category for "Popular Film"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Outstanding_Achievement_in_Popular_Film "Academy Award for Outstanding Achievement in Popular Film") in [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/91st_Academy_Awards "91st Academy Awards").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-33)

### Reduction

The two Lifetime Achievement Awards (the [Cecil B. DeMille Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Cecil_B._DeMille_Award "Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award") and the [Carol Burnett Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Carol_Burnett_Award "Golden Globe Carol Burnett Award")) were not presented this year, but expected to return in the future. Executive Vice President Tim Gray explained that with the change in ownership and status, and 25 of the competitive categories expanding from 5 nominees to 6, the increase will also include a reduction with no presentation of the two aforementioned awards for this year. "This is not a permanent change, with future awards slated to be given," Gray wrote in a post on the Globes' official website.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-34)

## Reception

### Criticism of Jo Koy's opening monologue

| External videos | |
| --- | --- |
| [![video icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg/20px-Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nuvola_apps_kaboodle.svg) [Jo Koy Opening Monologue \| 81st Annual Golden Globes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KvSHHnucouo) | |
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Jo_Koy_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg/250px-Jo_Koy_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jo_Koy_by_Gage_Skidmore.jpg)[Jo Koy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Koy "Jo Koy"), host of the 81st Golden Globe Awards

Host [Jo Koy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Koy "Jo Koy")'s opening [monologue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monologue "Monologue") was met with criticism from viewers and critics with many describing his jokes as "cringeworthy", "painful", and "unfunny". Chelsey Sanchez of *[Harper's Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's_Bazaar "Harper's Bazaar")* described the monologue as "awkward" and "distasteful".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-35) Koy was also criticized for putting blame on his writers during the monologue, coming after the lengthy [2023 Writers Guild of America strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike "2023 Writers Guild of America strike"). Justin Curto of *[Vulture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture_(website) "Vulture (website)")* noted that when some of his jokes fell flat, Koy "immediately threw his writers under the bus... He yelled. 'Yo, shut up. You're kidding me, right. Slow down. I wrote some of these and they're the ones you're laughing at'".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-36) Marlow Stern of *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* noted that many of Koy's jokes drew "groans" and "boos" from the audience.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-37)

Among jokes that drew the most ire were those about the film *[Barbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbie_(film) "Barbie (film)")*, and attending nominees [Robert De Niro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_De_Niro "Robert De Niro"), [Meryl Streep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meryl_Streep "Meryl Streep") and [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"); the latter's reaction went viral.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-40) Shirley Li of *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")* wrote: "Practically every joke failed to land, mostly because the punchlines were dated or obvious."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-41) Nicole Sperling of *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, who was in the audience that night, wrote that she had "never seen an audience rebel against an emcee so quickly" and cited a prominent film director describing the monologue as a "disaster".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-42)

Conversely, four-time [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") host and comedian [Whoopi Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whoopi_Goldberg "Whoopi Goldberg") defended Koy on *[The View](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View "The View")*, saying: "These hosting gigs are brutal. They're just brutal. If you don't know the room, if you've not been in these rooms before and you're sort of thrust out there, it's hit or miss. Now, I love Jo Koy, he makes me crazy because he's funny. I don't know whether it was the room, I don't know whether it was the jokes, I didn't get to see it. But I do know, that he is as good as it gets when it comes to stand-ups and it is not an easy gig."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-43) Actor and comedian [Steve Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Martin "Steve Martin") also threw his support behind Koy on [Threads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threads_(social_network) "Threads (social network)"), writing: "I tip my hat to anyone who steps out on stage to host a live awards show. It's a very difficult job and not for the squeamish. I know because I'm still throwing up from the last time I did it in 2010. So, Congratulations to Jo Koy, who took on the toughest gig in show business, hit, missed, was light on his feet, and now has twenty minutes of new material for his stand up!"[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-44)

Additionally, comedian [Michael Che](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Che "Michael Che") supported Koy by writing that "comedians should boycott hosting award shows" on [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-45) When questioned about Koy's jokes aimed toward her film *Barbie*, director [Greta Gerwig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Gerwig "Greta Gerwig") replied that she was not offended.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-46) On *[Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watch_What_Happens_Live_with_Andy_Cohen "Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen")*, actor and comedian [Kevin Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Hart "Kevin Hart") said he has "no reaction" to the backlash and went on to praise Koy for being a "phenomenal comedian".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-47) In a [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") post by Filipino actor and comedian [Michael V.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_V. "Michael V."), he posted: "I think Jo Koy's Golden Globes jokes are funny, direct, and pretty much self-explanatory. The last thing Jo Koy should be doing is trying to explain it to people who purposely choose NOT to understand and appreciate them."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-48)

Koy responded to the criticism in an interview with *[Good Morning America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Morning_America "Good Morning America")*, admitting: "I'd be lying if [I said] it doesn't hurt," but also admitted, "I had fun. You know, it was a moment that I'll always remember. Hosting is just a tough gig. Yes, I'm a stand-up comic, but that hosting position it's a different style. I kind of went in and did the writer's thing. We had ten days to write this monologue. It was a crash course. I feel bad, but I got to still say I loved what I did."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-49) In his first stand-up set afterward, Koy mocked the Hollywood celebrities, alluding: "Lot a marshmallows, man. They're delicious, but goddamn, they're soft. I just come from a different time. I see the changes that are happening. I get it, but goddamn, can we fucking laugh at ourselves?"[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_Golden_Globes#cite_note-50)

The **82nd Golden Globe Awards** was an awards ceremony that honored [excellence in film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_film "2024 in film") and [American television productions of 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_in_American_television "2024 in American television"). The winners were revealed during the live telecast, airing on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") and streaming on [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") on January 5, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-2) The event was hosted by comedian [Nikki Glaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Glaser "Nikki Glaser"), making her the first solo female host in Golden Globes history.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Glaser-3)

The nominations were announced live on December 9, 2024, at a [press conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_conference "Press conference") at [the Beverly Hilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beverly_Hilton "The Beverly Hilton") by actors [Morris Chestnut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Chestnut "Morris Chestnut") and [Mindy Kaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindy_Kaling "Mindy Kaling"), following an introduction from Golden Globes president, Helen Hoenhe.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Globes-4) *[Emilia Pérez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilia_Pérez "Emilia Pérez")*, with 10 nominations, became the most nominated comedy/musical film in [Golden Globes history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Awards#Superlatives "Golden Globe Awards"), just 1 shy of the overall record of 11, set by [Robert Altman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Altman "Robert Altman")'s [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") [satire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire_(film_and_television) "Satire (film and television)") *[Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_(film) "Nashville (film)")* in the drama category in [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Golden_Globe_Awards "33rd Golden Globe Awards").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-5) *[The Brutalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Brutalist "The Brutalist")* received the second-most in film with 7 nominations, followed by *[Conclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conclave_(film) "Conclave (film)")* with 6.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-6) Additionally, *[The Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bear_(TV_series) "The Bear (TV series)")* led the television nominations with 5, followed by *[Only Murders in the Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Only_Murders_in_the_Building "Only Murders in the Building")* and *[Shōgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shōgun_(2024_TV_series) "Shōgun (2024 TV series)")* with 4 each.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Variety-7)

## Ceremony information

On August 28, 2024, comedian [Nikki Glaser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Glaser "Nikki Glaser") was announced as the host for this year's ceremony, following last year's widely criticized host, comedian [Jo Koy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Koy "Jo Koy").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Glaser-3) She is the first woman to host the Golden Globes solo.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-8) Glaser herself was nominated for [Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Performance_in_Stand-Up_Comedy_on_Television "Golden Globe Award for Best Performance in Stand-Up Comedy on Television") for her [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") comedy special, *Nikki Glaser: Someday You'll Die*,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Governors-9) but lost to [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix")'s *Ali Wong: Single Lady*.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-10)

The ceremony was held at 5:00 p.m. [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Time_Zone "Pacific Time Zone") / 8:00 p.m. [EST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on January 5, 2025. It was broadcast live on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS") and streamed on [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Globes-4) [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") and [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") of White Cherry Entertainment returned from last year to executive produce the ceremony, along with [Dick Clark Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Clark_Productions "Dick Clark Productions").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Globes-4)

On December 3, 2024, it was announced that the two Lifetime Achievement Awards, which were not presented last year, would return this year; however, they were presented during an untelevised gala dinner on January 3, 2025, prior to the telecast, similar to the [Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards")' [Governors Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_Awards "Governors Awards").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Governors-9) The recipient of the [Cecil B. DeMille Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Cecil_B._DeMille_Award "Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award") was [Viola Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_Davis "Viola Davis"), while the [Carol Burnett Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Carol_Burnett_Award "Golden Globe Carol Burnett Award") was awarded to [Ted Danson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Danson "Ted Danson").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-11)

Aside from "El Mal", they were also jointly nominated for composing *Emilia Pérez*'s [Best Original Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Original_Score "Golden Globe Award for Best Original Score") and an additional Best Original Song nominee: "[Mi camino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_camino "Mi camino")".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Variety-7)

This year's nominations were tabulated by [KPMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPMG "KPMG"), the U.S. audit, tax, and advisory firm, taking over [Ernst & Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_&_Young "Ernst & Young") after fifty plus years.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Globes-4)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-15) [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") received a total of 36 nominations between film and television, the most of any distributor.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-16)

*Emilia Pérez* is the first non-English-language film (with some parts of English in the film) to win [Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Motion_Picture_–_Musical_or_Comedy "Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy"). *[Flow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_(2024_film) "Flow (2024 film)")* is the first [Latvian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvian_language "Latvian language") film to win [Best Animated Feature Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Animated_Feature_Film "Golden Globe Award for Best Animated Feature Film").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-17) [Fernanda Torres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernanda_Torres "Fernanda Torres") became the first [Brazilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_Portuguese "Brazilian Portuguese") actress to win a Golden Globe in an acting category,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Torres-18) as well as the first Brazilian, first [South American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") and first [Portuguese-speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language") actor to win the [Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actress_in_a_Motion_Picture_–_Drama "Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Drama").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Torres-18) She acknowledged her mother [Fernanda Montenegro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernanda_Montenegro "Fernanda Montenegro")'s nomination, for *[Central Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Station_(film) "Central Station (film)")* (1998), in the same category at the [56th Golden Globe Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56th_Golden_Globe_Awards "56th Golden Globe Awards").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Torres-18)

*Emilia Pérez* and *[Shōgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shōgun_(2024_TV_series) "Shōgun (2024 TV series)")* were the biggest winners of the night, for film and television, respectively, with four wins each.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Winners-19) *[The Brutalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Brutalist "The Brutalist")* was the next biggest film recipient, with three wins; for television, *[Baby Reindeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Reindeer "Baby Reindeer")* and *[Hacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacks_(TV_series) "Hacks (TV series)")* each won two.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Golden_Globes#cite_note-Winners-19)

Based on the official list of U.S. Secretaries of Education, here are all the individuals who held the position from the beginning of 2018 through the end of 2024, including acting secretaries:

| Secretary | Term of Office | Notes |
|-----------|----------------|-------|
| **Betsy DeVos** | February 7, 2017 – January 8, 2021 | Served as the 14th Secretary of Education under President Donald Trump. She resigned effective January 8, 2021【1†L1-L8】【2†L1-L6】. |
| **Mick Zais** (Acting) | January 8, 2021 – January 20, 2021 | Served as acting Secretary of Education immediately after DeVos’s resignation, during the transition period before the inauguration【3†L1-L4】【3†L5-L7】. |
| **Phil Rosenfelt** (Acting) | January 20, 2021 – March 2, 2021 | Served as acting Secretary of Education while the Biden administration’s nominee was being confirmed【4†L1-L4】【4†L5-L7】. |
| **Miguel Cardona** | March 2, 2021 – January 20, 2025 | Served as the 12th confirmed Secretary of Education under President Joe Biden, holding the position throughout 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024【5†L1-L4】【5†L5-L7】. |

**Summary:**  
- **Betsy DeVos** was the sitting Secretary for the entirety of 2018, 2019, and 2020, and remained in office until January 8, 2021.  
- **Mick Zais** and **Phil Rosenfelt** served as short-term acting Secretaries in January 2021.  
- **Miguel Cardona** was the confirmed Secretary for the remainder of the period, from March 2, 2021 through the end of 2024.

*Note: Linda McMahon was nominated in November 2024 and sworn in on March 3, 2025, so she was not in office during 2024.*

The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")'s [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

pergunta: Você pode listar todos os secretários de Saúde e Serviços Humanos dos EUA do início de 2018 até o fim de 2024, incluindo secretários interinos?
resposta:
Com base na lista oficial do Departamento de Saúde e Serviços Humanos (HHS) dos Estados Unidos, aqui está a lista completa de todos os Secretários de Saúde e Serviços Humanos (incluindo os secretários interinos) que atuaram do início de 2018 até o final de 2024:

---

### **Secretários de HHS (2018–2024)**

| # | Nome | Status | Período de Mandato | Observações |
|---|------|--------|-------------------|-------------|
| 1 | **Eric Hargan** | **Interino** | 10 de outubro de 2017 – 29 de janeiro de 2018 | Serviu como Secretário interino entre a renúncia de Tom Price e a nomeação de Alex Azar. |
| 2 | **Norris Cochran** | **Interino** | 20 de janeiro de 2017 – 10 de fevereiro de 2018 | Também serviu como interino entre Tom Price e Alex Azar, cobrindo o período até o início de 2018. |
| 3 | **Alex Azar** | Confirmado | 29 de janeiro de 2018 – 20 de janeiro de 2021 | Nomeado por Donald Trump e confirmado pelo Senado. |
| 4 | **Xavier Becerra** | Confirmado | 19 de março de 2021 – 20 de janeiro de 2025 | Nomeado por Joe Biden e confirmado pelo Senado. |

---

### **Detalhamento e contexto**

1. **Eric Hargan** e **Norris Cochran** foram os únicos secretários interinos durante o período solicitado. Ambos atuaram como chefes interinos entre a saída de **Tom Price** (que renunciou em 29 de setembro de 2017) e a entrada em exercício de **Alex Azar** (29 de janeiro de 2018). The **United States secretary of health and human services** is the head of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"), and serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on health matters. The secretary is a member of the [United States Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet "United States Cabinet"). [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the incumbent secretary of health and human services, having held the position since February 13, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-2)

The office was formerly known as the secretary of health, education, and welfare. In 1980, the [Department of Health, Education, and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") was renamed to Department of Health and Human Services, and its education functions and [Rehabilitation Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehabilitation_Services_Administration "Rehabilitation Services Administration") were transferred to the new [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-3) [Patricia Roberts Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Roberts_Harris "Patricia Roberts Harris") headed the department before and after it was renamed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-4)

Nominations to the office are referred to the [Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor,_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions") and the [United States Senate Committee on Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"), which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) before confirmation is considered by the full [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of health and human services is a [level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6) thus earning a salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar")250,600, as of January 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-Salary-7)

## Duties

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png/250px-Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare.png)The flag of the secretary of health, education, and welfare, the predecessor to the current office

The duties of the secretary revolve around human conditions and concerns in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). This includes advising the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on matters of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security "Social security"), and income security programs. The secretary strives to administer the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out approved programs and make the public aware of the objectives of the department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

The [Department of Health, Education and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") (HEW) was reorganized into a [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") and a [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS).

The Department of Health and Human Services oversees 11 agencies including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") (CDC), [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") (ACF) and [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of health and human services is as follows:[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-11)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services").
2. General Counsel of the Department of Health and Human Services
3. Assistant Secretary for Administration
4. [Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_for_Planning_and_Evaluation "Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation")
5. Administrator of the [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services")
6. [Commissioner of Food and Drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_Food_and_Drugs "Commissioner of Food and Drugs")
7. Director of the [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health")
8. Assistant Secretary for [Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families")
9. Other assistant secretaries (following in the order they took the oath of office)
  1. [Assistant Secretary for Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Assistant_Secretary_for_Health "United States Assistant Secretary for Health")
  2. [Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Assistant_Secretary_for_Preparedness_and_Response "Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response")
  3. Assistant Secretary for Legislation
  4. Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs
  5. Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources
  6. Assistant Secretary for [Aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_on_Aging "Administration on Aging")
10. Director of the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention")
11. Director, Region 4 ([Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"))

# [2404.08191] Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.08191) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1)
> Abstract:Multilingual pretraining has been a successful solution to the challenges posed by the lack of resources for languages. These models can transfer knowledge to target languages with minimal or no examples. Recent research suggests that monolingual models also have a similar capability, but the mechanisms behind this transfer remain unclear. Some studies have explored factors like language contamination and syntactic similarity. An emerging line of research suggests that the representations learned by language models contain two components: a language-specific and a language-agnostic component. The latter is responsible for transferring a more universal knowledge. However, there is a lack of comprehensive exploration of these properties across diverse target languages. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment inspired by the work on the Scaling Laws for Transfer. We measured the amount of data transferred from a source language to a target language and found that models initialized from diverse languages perform similarly to a target language in a cross-lingual setting. This was surprising because the amount of data transferred to 10 diverse target languages, such as Spanish, Korean, and Finnish, was quite similar. We also found evidence that this transfer is not related to language contamination or language proximity, which strengthens the hypothesis that the model also relies on language-agnostic knowledge. Our experiments have opened up new possibilities for measuring how much data represents the language-agnostic representations learned during pretraining.

## Submission history

# Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes

Thales Sales Almeida Affiliation: IC, UNICAMP, Brazil Affiliation: Maritaca AI, Brazil Roberto Lotufo Affiliation: FEEC, UNICAMP, Brazil Affiliation: NeuralMind, Brazil Rodrigo Nogueira Affiliation: FEEC, UNICAMP, Brazil Affiliation: Maritaca AI, Brazil

###### Abstract

Multilingual pretraining has been a successful solution to the challenges posed by the lack of resources for languages. These models can transfer knowledge to target languages with minimal or no examples. Recent research suggests that monolingual models also have a similar capability, but the mechanisms behind this transfer remain unclear. Some studies have explored factors like language contamination and syntactic similarity. An emerging line of research suggests that the representations learned by language models contain two components: a language-specific and a language-agnostic component. The latter is responsible for transferring a more universal knowledge. However, there is a lack of comprehensive exploration of these properties across diverse target languages. To investigate this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment inspired by the work on the Scaling Laws for Transfer. We measured the amount of data transferred from a source language to a target language and found that models initialized from diverse languages perform similarly to a target language in a cross-lingual setting. This was surprising because the amount of data transferred to 10 diverse target languages, such as Spanish, Korean, and Finnish, was quite similar. We also found evidence that this transfer is not related to language contamination or language proximity, which strengthens the hypothesis that the model also relies on language-agnostic knowledge. Our experiments have opened up new possibilities for measuring how much data represents the language-agnostic representations learned during pretraining.11 1 The code used in our experiments is publicly available at <https://github.com/lersouza/language-transfer>. We rely on the mC4 dataset from Huggingface, available at <https://huggingface.co/datasets/mc4>

## 1 Introduction

The emergence of self-supervised pretraining models such as BERT has revealed a notable phenomenon of cross-lingual transfer even when these models are trained on multilingual corpora devoid of paired translation examples. For example, LLAMA [Touvron et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib22 ""), which was trained self-supervisedly on an English-centric corpus, exhibits surprising multilingual capabilities [Yuan et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib28 ""); [Ye et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib27 "").
The underlying mechanisms driving this behavior remain unclear, with hypotheses ranging from the presence of shared “anchor” tokens [Pires et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib16 "") to language contamination [Blevins and Zettlemoyer (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib4 ""), yet no scientific consensus has been reached.

Research in this area often involves the use of pre-existing language models (LMs), which are subsequently finetuned on supervised datasets in different languages [de Souza et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib8 ""); [Yuan et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib28 ""). However, when evaluating multiple languages, conventional methodologies encounter two significant challenges: firstly, the dependence on supervised finetuning datasets, which often vary in size and quality, complicating cross-lingual comparisons; secondly, the use of subword tokenizers, which do not represent all languages equally.

In this work, we avoid these problems by working with a byte-level tokenizer and by using auto-regressive language models trained in self-supervised from scratch in one language and then finetuned on another.
To measure the effect of transfer learning, we employ the concept of data transfer [Hernandez et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib11 ""), which allows us to quantify how much each different source language contributes to the perplexity of the target language.

Our main contribution is providing a method that measures how much knowledge, in bytes, is transferred from one language to another. By applying it, our findings reveal a surprising trend: even when comparing linguistically distant languages, the data transfer metrics are of a comparable magnitude.
This research contributes additional evidence supporting the language-agnostic hypothesis, which suggests that the internal representations developed by a model are not only influenced by the linguistic surface form but also by the cultural and semantic content of the training data.

## 2 Related Work

Prior work attributed the success of multilingual models in cross-lingual transfer to “anchor” tokens [Pires et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib16 ""). However, subsequent research demonstrated that models could perform well even without these tokens [Artetxe et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib2 ""), highlighting the significance of shared parameters during training [Conneau et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib7 ""). Competitive results were achieved by monolingual models with minimal or no adaptation [Artetxe et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib2 ""); [de Souza et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib8 "").

Investigations by [Blevins and Zettlemoyer (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib4 "") linked these findings to language contamination, where pretraining datasets contained target language data. Additional factors contributing to cross-lingual transfer success include dataset statistics, language attributes [Lin et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib13 ""), language structure [Lin et al. (2019)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib13 ""); [Papadimitriou and Jurafsky (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib15 ""); [Chiang and yi Lee (2020)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib6 ""); [Ri and Tsuruoka (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib18 ""), and token overlap between training and target languages [Beukman and Fokam (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib3 ""). The role of language script [Fujinuma et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib9 "") and model tokenizer [Rust et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib20 "") was also noted, prompting the use of a byte tokenizer to address these issues [Xue et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib25 ""); [Abonizio et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib1 "").

Recent research proposed a two-component model representation hypothesis—language agnostic and language specific [de Souza et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib8 ""); [Zeng et al. (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib29 ""); [Wu et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib24 ""). While promising, no study has measured how much of the language-agnostic component is used in settings with multiple source and target languages. Additionally, existing research still applies the source language vocabulary to the target language, potentially compromising input representations and affecting results.

To address these gaps, we draw on [Hernandez et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib11 "") and employ a byte vocabulary in our experiments to overcome current literature limitations.

## 3 Methodology

Inspired by [Hernandez et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib11 ""), our methodology focuses on quantifying the transferability of pretraining data across distributions, particularly between different languages. We select a target language and finetune models initialized from various source languages onto it. Subsequently, we evaluate each model on a target language test set and compare their performance. We introduce the Data Transfer (<!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="D_{T}" display="inline" id="S3.p1.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T}) metric to estimate knowledge transfer, explained in more depth in [3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S3.SS1 "3.1 Data Transfer Estimation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes").
This process is repeated across different target languages to observe effects across a broad linguistic spectrum.

These experiments aim to quantify and compare cross-lingual knowledge transfer from different source languages. This analysis seeks to uncover the extent to which transferability depends on specific languages and the importance of language-agnostic components in learned representations. The following sections provide further details.

### 3.1 Data Transfer Estimation

![SVG Image](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)Figure 1: Example illustrating how the coeficients <!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.F1.m9"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T}, <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="D_{F}" id="S3.F1.m10"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DFD_{F} and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.F1.m11"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{E}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DED_{E} are calculated. Each series represents a different initialization. <!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{T}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.F1.m12"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} is the number of additional tokens in the target language that a from-scratch model would have needed to achieve the same perplexity of a model finetuned from English. <!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.F1.m13"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DFD_{F} is the size of the dataset used for finetuning and <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="D_{E}" display="inline" id="S3.F1.m14"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{E}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DED_{E} accounts for all data, both <!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.F1.m15"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DFD_{F} and <!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{T}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.F1.m16"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T}.

To quantify the knowledge transfer from pretrained models to a given target language, we utilize the Data Transfer (<!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="D_{T}" id="S3.SS1.p1.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T}) metric. This metric assesses the effectiveness of pretraining data by measuring the additional tokens required in the target language for a model initialized from scratch to match the performance of a model pretrained on a source language and finetuned on the target. Figure [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Data Transfer Estimation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes") illustrates this concept.

### 3.2 Task and Evaluation Metric

We adopt Language Modeling as our main task with perplexity as the performance metric for all experiments. Perplexity, derived from the model’s loss (<!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="e^{loss}" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS2.p1.m1"><semantics><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{loss}</annotation></semantics></math> --> el​o​s​se^{loss}), facilitates future predictions of model behavior in transfer learning scenarios, following the approach in [Hernandez et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib11 ""). This choice also allows extensive experiments across multiple languages, leveraging datasets like mC4 [Xue et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib26 "") to overcome size limitations inherent in supervised datasets.

### 3.3 Tokenization Impact

In cross-lingual setups, the choice of tokenization method holds considerable significance [Rust et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib20 ""). While subword tokenizers are commonly employed in cross-lingual experiments, using a tokenizer trained in a source language on a distant target language may result in an increased number of tokens. This can lead to the utilization of undertrained embeddings in some instances, introducing challenges for effective sentence representation. Furthermore, dealing with different scripts introduces the issue of numerous “unknown” tokens, exacerbating the difficulty of obtaining suitable input representations for the model.

To address these challenges, we opt for a byte vocabulary based on the approach proposed by [Xue et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib25 ""), which allows us to standardize representations across all languages, ensuring that each model encounters the same quantity of UTF-8 bytes. By doing so, we mitigate the use of unknown tokens and undertrained embeddings, thereby minimizing the impact of tokenization issues on the performance of our experiments.

### 3.4 Language Contamination

A potential reason for a pretrained model’s superior performance in cross-lingual tasks is the presence of a substantial amount of data in the target language in its pretraining dataset, a phenomenon referred to as language contamination. To quantify this impact, following the approach outlined by [Blevins and Zettlemoyer (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib4 ""), we examine the rates of target language fragments in the source language dataset and vice versa.

Specifically, for a given source language <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="\ell" display="inline" id="S3.SS4.p2.m1"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> --> ℓ\ell and target language <!-- MathML: <math alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS4.p2.m2"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> --> tt, we calculate the ratio of all lines classified as <!-- MathML: <math alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS4.p2.m3"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> --> ℓ\ell in the target dataset (known as contamination on target) and as <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="t" id="S3.SS4.p2.m4"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> --> tt in the pretraining dataset (known as contamination on source). We perform language detection using the fasttext tool ([Bojanowski et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib5 "")), employing a threshold of 0.6 for classification.

Next, we compute the Spearman correlation between the set of Data Transfer metrics <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="\mathbf{D_{T}}" id="S3.SS4.p3.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐃</mi><mi>𝐓</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D_{T}}</annotation></semantics></math> --> 𝐃𝐓\mathbf{D_{T}} and those ratios obtained from the outcomes of our experiments.

Correlating these rates with the model’s data transfer indicator allows us to evaluate the impact of language contamination on model performance.

### 3.5 Language Similarity

Language similarity is often cited as a crucial factor influencing cross-lingual transfer performance in natural language processing tasks. In this work, we aim to investigate the relationship between language similarity and cross-lingual transfer effectiveness based on the outcomes of our experiments.

To explore this relationship, we measure various distances between languages, including syntactic, geographic, and phonological distances. These distances are calculated based on the methodology proposed by [Littell et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib14 "").

We aim to correlate these language distances with the data transfer metric (<!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S3.SS5.p3.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T}). By employing Spearman correlation analysis, we seek to discern whether there exists a significant correlation between the observed <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="D_{T}" display="inline" id="S3.SS5.p3.m2"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} values and the measured language distances.

This analysis elucidates whether our experimental results can be attributed to the similarities between the languages involved in our cross-lingual experiments.

## 4 Experiments

This section presents the languages, datasets, model architecture, and training details for our experiments.

### 4.1 Languages

Source Languages Selection. We chose three diverse languages—English, Russian, and Chinese—for the source language during the pretraining phase. This selection ensures a broad linguistic spectrum while adhering to pretraining budget constraints.

Target Languages Selection. Ten target languages, spanning various language families and different scripts, were chosen to establish a diverse cross-lingual setting. Details, including language codes, are provided in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Languages ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes").

Table 1: Characteristics of selected target languages.

### 4.2 Datasets

For training and finetuning, language subsets from the mC4 dataset [Xue et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib26 "") for the selected languages were utilized.33 3 See <https://huggingface.co/datasets/mc4> for more details. Pretraining datasets comprised approximately 6 billion tokens, while finetuning datasets ranged from 6 million to 6 billion tokens. Documents were sampled at random without replacement until the desired amount of tokens was reached.

### 4.3 Model Architecture

Our model is a decoder-only Transformer [Vaswani et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib23 "") that uses a byte vocabulary with 256 embeddings with a dimension of 640. The model follows closely the implementation provided in the T5x library. It consists of 10 layers, each having 10 attention heads with dimensions of 64. The intermediate dimension of Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) has a dimension of 2560 and GELU [Hendrycks and Gimpel (2023)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib10 "") activations. The parameters of the embeddings matrix and the final dense layer are shared. We use relative positional embeddings [Shaw et al. (2018)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib21 ""). The resulting model has approximately 65 million parameters.

### 4.4 Training details

Models were trained using a causal language modeling objective. Each batch has 512 sequences of 1024 tokens. We use the AdamW optimizer with an initial learning rate of 2e-4, which decayed to 2e-5 through cosine decay following [Hoffmann et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib12 ""). Finetuning employed a constant learning rate of 2e-5 over 10 epochs, except for the 6 billion dataset size where we limited it to 3 epochs. This adjustment was based on preliminary experiments indicating that the model tends to overfit beyond this epoch count in larger datasets. The best model was selected based on the lowest perplexity achieved on the development set. Warmup steps varied with finetuning dataset sizes (ranging from 0 for smaller datasets to 3000 for larger ones), aligning with findings that smaller datasets completed finetuning before warmup completion [Hernandez et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib11 ""). We utilized the T5X framework [Roberts et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib19 "") for our experiments. We used a total of 600 hours of a TPU v2-8 (seven hours of pretraining per model, and fifteen hours for the largest finetuning).

### 5.1 Performance with different initializations

We delve into the results of three target languages: Spanish, Arabic, and Japanese. The perplexity scores across all dataset sizes for these languages are highlighted in Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1 Performance with different initializations ‣ 5 Results ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes"), offering a chance for in-depth analysis despite the constraints of space.

A key observation is the consistent proximity of perplexity values for all three source languages in every target language. For instance, while one might expect a significant advantage for Chinese as a source language when finetuned in Japanese, or for English when paired with Spanish, this is not the case. This suggests the model leverages source language representations even when it lacks significant similarity with the target language.

Taken together, our results indicate that the model can rely on representations beyond those capturing language structure. This observation supports the recent hypothesis that these representations encompass both language-specific and language-neutral components, strengthening the latter as an important aspect.

Analysis of the Data Transfer (<!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS2.p1.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T}) metric in Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes") reveals that values are consistently close across different source languages for a given target. Notable examples include Arabic (en: 101MB, ru: 99MB, zh: 90MB), Japanese (en: 47.5MB, ru: 47.8MB, zh: 69.48MB), and Finnish (en: 102.62MB, ru: 51.32MB, zh: 76.57MB).

A clear pattern emerges: one initialization stands out for most target languages, while the other two show similar <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="D_{T}" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS2.p2.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} values. This pattern is visually represented in Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Data Transfer estimation for target languages ‣ 5 Results ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes"), particularly evident for Finnish (fi), Indonesian (id), Japanese (ja), Korean (ko), and Chinese (zh). Additionally, closely clustered results are observed for Arabic (ar), German (de), Spanish (es), and Russian (ru).

With three diverse initializations, the fact that two consistently show similar <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="D_{T}" id="S5.SS2.p3.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} values, even when distant from the target language (e.g., Russian and Chinese for Finnish), suggests the models leverage language-agnostic representations. This observation aligns with the expected behavior, where <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="D_{T}" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS2.p3.m2"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} would be close to zero if language-specific knowledge were dominant.

English (en) demonstrates effective knowledge transfer to most target languages, potentially due to its widespread presence in corpora across languages. This hypothesis is explored further in Section [5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S5.SS3 "5.3 Language Contamination Impact ‣ 5 Results ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes"). Additionally, Chinese (zh) appears to transfer effectively to Japanese (ja) and Korean (ko), likely due to their linguistic proximity.

We observe that Chinese (zh) tends to transfer effectively to Japanese (ja) and Korean (ko), both of which are considered closer languages. This, together with our other observations, indicates that, while not determinant, language-specific component also plays a role in cross-lingual transfer.

## 6 Discussion

Our study aims to measure how much knowledge, in bytes, is transferred from one language to another, enabling the investigation of the effectiveness of language-agnostic representations acquired during pretraining in cross-lingual scenarios. We hypothesize that these representations enable models to perform well on downstream tasks across diverse languages, which is observed in state-of-the-art multilingual models.

In our results, we consistently find that at least two source languages demonstrate very close <!-- MathML: <math alttext="D_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S6.p2.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} values when evaluated against a target language, despite the diverse set of script systems and linguistic characteristics involved. This observation suggests that the data transferred from these languages to the target language is not primarily related to language-specific components but rather to language-agnostic ones. For instance, as illustrated in Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Data Transfer estimation for target languages ‣ 5 Results ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes"), both English and Russian, despite being known as distant languages, achieve nearly identical <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="D_{T}" id="S6.p2.m2"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} values when evaluated on Korean, a language distinct from either. Moreover, all three source languages are remarkably close when evaluated on the Japanese test set.

Despite exposure to only a few tokens in the target language, our models demonstrate similar perplexity performance, indicating high adaptability and generalization across a broad range of languages. This reinforces the notion that the language-agnostic component plays a crucial, uniform role across source languages.

Notably, our results are not attributed to pretraining exposure to target languages, since there is a weak correlation of language contamination with the data transfer coefficient. Additionally, the observed performance is not solely dependent on language proximity, as suggested in other works.

While perplexity offers valuable insights, generalizable conclusions require evaluation in downstream tasks, especially in under-resourced languages. To explore this further, we conducted a small-scale experiment, detailed in Appendix [A](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#A1 "Appendix A Appendix: Downstream Task Experiment ‣ Measuring Cross-lingual Transfer in Bytes"), finetuning our pretrained models for a low-resource language inference task. Surprisingly, we observe comparable accuracy scores between Portuguese and Russian, with good results also for English and Chinese, suggesting that our initial findings with perplexity may extend broadly. However, a more detailed investigation is required to understand cross-lingual transfer mechanisms fully.

The novelty of our approach is employing a byte-level tokenizer and adapting [Hernandez et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib11 "") for a cross-lingual scenario. The byte-level approach facilitates consistent model embeddings across diverse scripts, enabling effective cross-lingual knowledge transfer without language-specific tokenization or preprocessing. This is supported by the strong performance of ByT5 compared to mT5 in [Xue et al. (2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib25 "").

In conclusion, our study suggests the presence of language-agnostic representations contributing to cross-lingual transferability, while also laying the foundation to measure it through the Data Transfer metric. The observed consistency in model performance across diverse languages, facilitated by the byte-level tokenizer, indicates the potential for more efficient and generalizable natural language understanding across linguistic boundaries in computational linguistics and NLP.

## 7 Limitations

Our study has certain limitations that merit consideration. Firstly, our choice of initializing models with only three languages, while diverse, leaves room for improvement. Including additional languages in the pretraining phase would enhance the robustness of our analysis by minimizing possible bias towards the selected languages while providing more samples for our correlation analysis. However, this expansion would necessitate a more substantial computational budget.

Secondly, our reliance on small models, specifically a 65 million parameter model, limits the scope of our findings as larger models may exhibit different behavior. Additionally, the capacity of very large models for few-shot learning opens avenues for further exploration in the domain of transfer learning.

Lastly, the heterogeneity of the mC4 dataset across languages introduces a potential source of variability in the models’ exposure to different knowledge. While the impact of this variation on data transfer remains unclear, conducting experiments with controlled datasets would offer valuable insights. Moreover, employing a more comparable test set could help mitigate statistical variance, particularly in analyses such as the commutative property assessment.

## 8 Conclusion and Future Work

Our study delves into the transferability of knowledge in cross-lingual scenarios, leveraging a byte-level tokenizer and an adapted methodology inspired by [Hernandez et al. (2021)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08191v1#bib.bib11 ""). By measuring the models’ reliance on pretraining when executing tasks in diverse languages, our approach offers an understanding of the cross-lingual capabilities of language models. The results provide evidence that language-agnostic representations also play an important role in downstream tasks. This not only contributes to the current understanding of cross-lingual transferability but also serves as a catalyst for further exploration into the properties of language-agnostic knowledge transfer. For future research directions, we envision key investigations that can build upon the insights presented in this paper:

1. 1.     Expand Experiment Range: Use more source languages so we can draw stronger conclusions.

2. 2.     Controlled Datasets Usage: Employ controlled datasets and comparable test sets to address mC4 dataset heterogeneity, offering clearer insights into varied knowledge exposure impact on cross-lingual transferability and mitigating variance.

3. 3.     Explore Larger Models: Investigate the use of larger models in few-shot learning downstream tasks as complementary evaluations to perplexity measurements.

4. 4.     Measure <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="D_{T}" display="inline" id="S8.I1.i4.p1.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> --> DTD_{T} from Non-natural languages: Perform experiments with non-natural language data, such as artificial languages with hierarchical structures. This exploration could shed light on whether knowledge transfer primarily occurs due to the content of pretraining or is largely influenced by the linguistic form.
